title: Make the baseline table maintain itself, and stop tests breaking on its drift

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited 923f4c9 with bookkeeping c2c8b9b, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

This closes drift I first flagged in sprint 9's notes and raised again in sprints 10 and 14 — four occurrences before it got scheduled. Every requirement was demonstrated rather than read, including in the direction the criterion insists on.

================================================================
THE SAFETY-CRITICAL CHECK NOBODY ASKED FOR, DONE FIRST
================================================================

Regenerating this table is the single most dangerous operation in this project: sprint 8 established that a wrong hash here silently authorizes overwriting a file somebody edited. The criteria do not ask about it, so I checked it before anything else.

PRE-EXISTING HASHES CHANGED: 0. Compared every (path, version) pair in the old committed table (7442edb) against the new one: 63 hashes added, zero altered, coverage extended 0.1.0-0.1.8 to 0.1.0-0.1.17. Purely additive, which is the property that matters — a regeneration that quietly rewrote an old hash would be undetectable by eye and would authorize a destructive overwrite.

AND I DERIVED THE NEW HASHES INDEPENDENTLY, not from the generator. Downloaded the real published tarballs for 0.1.9, 0.1.13 and 0.1.17, extracted each tracked path, normalised CRLF and computed sha256 in my own Python — a separate implementation from content-hash.js. 21 hashes across three versions: 21 match, 0 mismatch. Sprint 8's standard ("verified by regenerating, not by reading") applied to the new rows, since those are the ones nobody has checked before.

================================================================
REQ 1 — BOTH DIRECTIONS, AND THE FAILING ONE IS THE POINT
================================================================

The criterion says a check verified only in the passing direction does not clear this. Ran both against the real registry:

  PASSING (current regenerated table):
    "OK: scripts/baselines/user-owned-content.json covers every published version (through 0.1.17)."  exit 0
  FAILING (restored the old stale table from 7442edb):
    "ERROR: ... is stale. Missing version(s): 0.1.9, 0.1.10, 0.1.11, 0.1.12, 0.1.13, 0.1.14, 0.1.15,
     0.1.16, 0.1.17. Table covers through 0.1.8; the registry's latest published version is 0.1.17.
     Run `node scripts/baselines/generate.js` (or `npm run baselines:generate`) and commit the result."  exit 1
It names every missing version, names what it covers, names the registry's latest, and names the remedy including both invocations. Restored, passes again. That failing message is what would have caught this four sprints ago.

THE N-1 RULE IS ENCODED, NOT ASSUMED, and encoded the right way. "Latest published" comes from generate.js's own publishedVersions() — a live registry query — not from package.json's version minus one. That distinction is load-bearing and the comment states it: package.json is already 0.1.18 while the table covers through 0.1.17, and the check passes, because 0.1.18 does not exist on the registry yet and cannot be demanded. A correct pre-release state does not trip it — demonstrated, since that is exactly the state this repo is in right now.

A consequence worth recording because it looks wrong until you think it through: every published package necessarily ships a table one version behind itself, since its own version does not exist at pack time. That is fine and self-correcting — an install upgrading from 0.1.18 to 0.1.19 is matched against 0.1.19's table, which does contain 0.1.18. Subtracting one locally would have been the obvious implementation and would have been wrong the first time a version was skipped or a publish failed.

================================================================
REQ 3 — I BROKE IT MYSELF TO CONFIRM IT NO LONGER BREAKS
================================================================

The criterion says to read the approach against the failure it must prevent, and that if a future edit to an agent file would still break a test it is not fixed. I did not read it; I reproduced the failure.

WHAT WAS COUPLED: the two baseline-match tests in launcher_test.js pinned a specific persona file that had to remain unedited — qa1.md originally, repointed to liveqa.md in sprint 9, then to pipeman.md, then to dev-team-1.md. Four sprints, four repointings, each one a sprint editing the file the tests happened to depend on.

WHAT IT IS COUPLED TO NOW: nothing specific. findBaselineProvenFile() scans every tracked path in the real table and picks the first whose current content still matches any recorded hash.

DEMONSTRATED: the currently-picked file is .claude/agents/dev-team-1.md. I appended a line to that exact file and re-ran the suite — ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, and the selection fell through to .claude/agents/dev-team-2.md. Restored, still passing. The recurring breakage is genuinely gone rather than moved to a different file.

The all-edited case is handled too, and handled well: it throws a named error saying every tracked file has been edited since the table was regenerated and to run `npm run baselines:generate`, rather than failing as a confusing assertion mismatch. That is the difference between a test that tells you what to do and one that sends you reading test internals.

================================================================
REQS 2, 4, 5 — MET
================================================================

Req 2 — both scripts exist (package.json's scripts block was previously empty, now baselines:generate and baselines:check), and the regeneration step is wired into pipeman.md at 9.3, placed after `npm publish` and before the bookkeeping commit. That placement is correct and non-obvious: it is the one moment the just-published version exists on the registry to be hashed, and it lands in the same commit sprint 9's ordering already reserved for bookkeeping. The check also runs inside verify-tarball.sh as its own section, so it sits in a path every release actually reaches rather than one someone has to remember.

Req 4 — package.json 0.1.18, one line.

Req 5 — ran the suite: 149 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED. The negative case is covered with deterministic fake data rather than depending on registry state, which is right for a unit test, and I exercised the real negative case separately above. verify-tarball.sh: TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.1.18 (first install)", and its new section reports the table current through 0.1.17.

================================================================
FOR MASTER CONTROLLER — THE STALE LiveQA CRITERION DEV TEAM FLAGGED
================================================================

Confirmed, and the sprint file contradicts itself about it. Line 59 says "confirm its baseline table covers through `0.1.16` — the release before this one." Line 74, in the same file, says the sequence is "0.1.16, 0.1.17 (sprint 17), then 0.1.18." Sprint 17 was sequenced ahead and shipped 0.1.17, so this release is 0.1.18 and the correct expectation is 0.1.17.

Not blocking and not Dev Team's — they flagged it and correctly did not edit a sprint file. But it should be corrected before LiveQA runs, or LiveQA checks a number that was right when the sprint was written and is not now. The mechanism itself does not depend on that sentence: check-staleness.js queries the live registry and hardcodes no version, which is why the drift in the prose has no effect on the code. That is the design working — the sentence went stale and the check could not.

Note the sequencing, since it has cost a round twice: amending the sprint file after this PASS changes qa1_audit_file_hash and /sprint-dev-done will refuse. Decide it deliberately rather than meeting it at dev-done.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. Carried, unchanged and still open: the CLI-version-drift item from sprint 17 — docs/sprint-12-permission-scope-findings.md records no `claude` version and one of its CONFIRMED entries has already expired. Sprint 16 is a good precedent for it: this sprint's whole answer to "a recorded fact silently went stale" was a mechanical check on a release path, which is exactly the shape that item needs.
2. Also carried: the --agents argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit; the interactive auth-check ordering from sprint 11 round 1; and sprint 17's bare-verb allowlist question (`Bash(npm publish *)` against a bare `npm publish`), which LiveQA should still settle.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 16, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.18 — and this is the first release where step 9.3 runs, so the table it regenerates should come back covering through 0.1.18. Then `verify-publish 16`.

Worth saying once: the failing-direction message this sprint added would have named 0.1.9 as missing the moment 0.1.9 published. It took four occurrences and three of my own notes to get scheduled, and the fix is a check that runs on every release path. That is the right trade and it is the last of the recurring items I have been carrying since sprint 9.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.18 on macOS and on a real Windows 11 ARM VM. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64; Windows 11 26100 ARM64 (user-run, encrypted VM, I hold no credentials). 2026-09-05.

All four criteria pass. No blocking findings. The drift this sprint exists to end was worse than my own sprint-9 note recorded, and it is now closed with the two safety properties that matter both demonstrated.

PROVENANCE
`npm view fully-completely version` -> 0.1.18; gitHead 6f08bad9b2918965e88947eefb71a1a7e3718754 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events. Per sprint 13's rule I also ran the content check: all 57 files in the published tarball byte-identical to `git show 6f08bad:<path>` (MISMATCHED 0, NOT-IN-COMMIT 0), and my tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum. Ran my own registry query before reading verify-publish's record.

================================================================
CRITERION 2 — THE PUBLISHED TABLE IS CURRENT: PASS, AND THE OLD STATE WAS WORSE THAN RECORDED
================================================================
The criterion asks that the published table cover through the release before this one. It does, and the comparison against its predecessor is the finding:

  shipped in 0.1.17:  covers 0.1.0 .. 0.1.8   (9 versions)   generatedAt 2026-09-01T06:22:21.049Z
  shipped in 0.1.18:  covers 0.1.0 .. 0.1.17  (18 versions)  generatedAt 2026-09-05T14:02:58.958Z

So as recently as 0.1.17 the shipped table was NINE releases stale — 0.1.9 through 0.1.17 all uncovered — still carrying the timestamp it had when I first flagged the drift at sprint 9's gate. My sprint-9 note recorded the uncovered range as 0.1.6-0.1.8; by 0.1.17 it had grown to nine versions, exactly as predicted, because nothing in the release path regenerated it. 0.1.18 closes it.

The in-repo table now covers through 0.1.18 (19 versions), written by the post-publish regeneration. That ordering is necessarily correct rather than sloppy: a published package cannot contain the hash of its own tarball, so the entry for release N can only exist after N is live. Step 9.3 running after publish confirmed is the only sequence that can work, and Pipeman ran it that way.

================================================================
CRITERION 3 — THE UPGRADE PATH STILL WORKS, AND REGENERATION ONLY ADDED: PASS
================================================================
The criterion's sharp edge is "a regenerated table must not change any existing hash — only add versions", because a silently altered hash is what would authorise overwriting somebody's edited file. Two independent checks.

ONLY-ADDITIONS, by diffing the two published tables entry by entry:
  pre-existing entries UNCHANGED:        63
  pre-existing entries altered/removed:   0
  newly added entries:                   63
Regeneration is purely additive. It cannot rewrite history.

EVERY HASH IS REAL, by recomputing rather than reading. Fetched all eighteen published tarballs and recomputed the CRLF-normalised sha256 of all seven tracked paths in every version, comparing against the shipped table:
  MATCHING 126   MISMATCHED 0   MISSING 0   TOTAL 126
Done independently of scripts/baselines/generate.js — I hashed the tarballs directly, so a bug in the generator could not hide from this check. Every hash in the table corresponds to real published content.

THE UPGRADE PATH ITSELF, on macOS, from a genuine pre-manifest install:
  installed published 0.1.2 (marker 0.1.2, manifest ABSENT — the true pre-manifest shape)
  "demonstrated, not argued" absent before (0)
  upgraded to published 0.1.18: exit 0, ZERO conflicts, 7 user-owned files replaced
  rule present after (1), manifest populated with 7 entries
The table is what proves those files untouched, and it did.

THE SAFETY PROPERTY, still holding on the new table: planted SENTINEL-S16-MUST-SURVIVE in a published-0.1.4 install's qa1.md, upgraded to 0.1.18. Hash identical before and after (1e5d08d0deb0a3b2), sentinel intact, and the file correctly ABSENT from the manifest (6 entries, not 7) because it matched nothing and is not proven untouched. A larger table did not make the destructive branch reachable.

================================================================
CRITERION 4 — macOS AND WINDOWS BOTH UNAFFECTED: PASS. WINDOWS WAS OBTAINABLE AND WAS USED.
================================================================
The criterion says to record plainly if a Windows machine cannot be obtained. One could be — the VM from sprints 10 and 14 was still running — so I used it rather than recording an untestability claim, which is the rule sprint 9 added and which I would be the wrong person to ignore.

Windows 11 ARM, same two checks:
  0.1.2 -> 0.1.18 upgrade: "Upgraded 0.1.2 -> 0.1.18", EXITCODE=0, ZERO conflicts, 26 files replaced
    with backups, including all six agent files and CLAUDE.md; rule present after (1)
  manifest: 7 entries, every key forward-slash (".claude/agents/qa1.md"), no backslashes —
    sprint 10's normalization still holding on the platform it was written for
  sentinel: PRE  = 6D42819B7003F77550CB17E1C8AE0BABAB6EBE190BA145C40E4C10064D1D0022
            POST = 6D42819B7003F77550CB17E1C8AE0BABAB6EBE190BA145C40E4C10064D1D0022
            SENTINEL COUNT 1, "RESULT: SAFE - not overwritten"
            manifest 6 entries with qa1.md ABSENT
Identical behaviour to macOS on both checks. Neither platform was fixed at the other's expense.

================================================================
INCIDENTAL — A MITIGATING FACT FOR MY OPEN SPRINT-17 FINDING
================================================================
At sprint 17's gate I recorded that readDeclaredTestCommand() injects `.vscode/settings.json`'s `fullyCompletely.testCommand` into the allowlist with no validation, so a declared value of "bash" or "node" silently unscopes dev-team-1, dev-team-2 and qa1.

This release's installer output shows it now writes that key itself, so I checked what default it writes. It writes the empty string (install.js:747), and readDeclaredTestCommand() returns null for an empty or whitespace value, so no allowlist entry is injected at all unless a project deliberately sets one.

That narrows the finding usefully and supports the call I made there. The hazard is not a default state and never arrives on its own — it requires a project to write a value, and only a badly-chosen value is dangerous. The finding stands (a validation step or a warning on a single-token interpreter would close it) but it is a configuration hazard, not a shipped exposure. Recording here because the fact only became visible in this release.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
The macOS runs, the provenance check, the table comparison and all 126 hash recomputations I ran directly. The Windows results come from the user's VM running the published 0.1.18 from the registry, driven by a suite I wrote and scored from the raw uploaded output; the user ran it because the VM is encrypted and I hold no credentials.

Pipeman's report arrived mid-run and changed nothing — its gitHead claim, its version-coverage claim and its account of step 9.3's ordering were all checked against the registry and the published tarballs rather than accepted. The specific claim I was asked to spot-check, that the table is current and stays clean, is confirmed and quantified above.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready, and this closes the drift I first flagged at sprint 9's gate — where I noted the table was stale and that nothing in the release path regenerated it, so it would go stale again on the very next release. It did, for nine of them. Wiring regeneration into step 9.3 is the fix that had to happen at the process layer rather than the code layer, and its first real exercise worked.

The two properties I would have failed this on both hold: regeneration added 63 entries and altered none, and all 126 hashes correspond to real published content. Windows and macOS behave identically.

No findings carry forward from this sprint. The sprint-17 testCommand validation item is unchanged but narrowed, as noted above.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 16.
